standards.name: Simulation Experiment Description Markup Language (SED-ML)
standards.abstract: SED-ML is a machine-readable standard for describing simulation experiments of computational models (e.g., SBML, CellML, BNGL) and the results to be recorded and exported. It is typically used inside COMBINE/OMEX archives alongside model files and visualization specifications (e.g., Vega) to make simulation experiments reproducible and portable across tools. The BioSimulations documentation presents SED-ML as the convention to declare which models to run, how to modify them, which simulation algorithms and settings to use, what observables to record and reduce, and how to output or visualize results; it also documents expectations for simulator support (a required subset of SED-ML L1V3 features) and how to link SED-ML outputs to Vega visualizations.

classification.rationale: The source material is prose guidance and a checklist of required/recommended elements and behaviors (e.g., what SED-ML should describe, which SED-ML elements containers should support, how to link SED-ML outputs to Vega). It lists items as instructions or capabilities rather than providing a row/column metadata table or an explicit ordered workflow DAG, so it is best represented as a set of principles.

principles.principle: When building Vega visualizations that consume SED-ML results, annotate Vega signals and data sets with sedmlUri keys to link to SED-ML documents, simulations/reports, and attributes.
principles.evidence: To set the value attribute of a Vega signal equal to the value of an attribute of a simulation or report of a SED-ML document, add a sedmlUri key to the signal with a value equal to a list of the location of the SED-ML document, the id of the SED-ML simulation or report, and the name of the attribute of the simulation or report (e.g., ['location/of/simulation.sedml', 'simulationId', 'numberOfSteps'] ).

principles.principle: Annotate Vega data sets with sedmlUri keys to render them with the results of SED-ML reports (supporting selection of all reports, or a single report).
principles.evidence: Annotate the Vega data sets whose values should be rendered with the results of SED-ML reports by adding sedmlUri keys to these Vega data sets. To render a Vega data set with the results of all reports from all of the SED-ML files in the parent COMBINE/OMEX archive, the value of the sedmlUri key should be an empty array (i.e. []). To render a Vega data set with the result of a single report from one SED-ML file in the parent COMBINE/OMEX archive, the value of the sedmlUri key should be a list of the location of the SED-ML document and the id of the report in the document (e.g., ['location/of/simulation.sedml', 'reportId']).

standards.name: COMBINE/OMEX archive format
standards.abstract: COMBINE/OMEX archives are zip-based containers used to package simulation projects: they bundle model files (e.g., SBML, BNGL, CellML), SED-ML experiment descriptions, visualizations, and other assets together with a manifest that records file formats. The BioSimulations documentation and utilities describe how COMBINE/OMEX archives are used to execute, validate, publish, and share simulation studies (including guidance for preparing archives, what to check before publishing, and how reports/plots in SED-ML map to output tables). The materials come from the BioSimulations project (runBioSimulations, BioSimulators utilities and test-suite examples) and address practical aspects of using COMBINE/OMEX archives with simulation tools: what the archive contains, how results are formatted, validation checks the platform performs, and recommended checks before publishing.

classification.rationale: The source materials are primarily prose guidance, instructions, and checklists (how to use, validate, and publish COMBINE/OMEX archives) rather than a field-level metadata schema or an ordered procedure. They contain recommendations and reporting/checklist items (e.g., what to verify before publishing, what the validator checks), so 'principle' best matches the structure.

principles.principle: COMBINE/OMEX archives are zip files with a manifest that indicates each file's format.
principles.evidence: BioSimulations supports the COMBINE/OMEX archive format. COMBINE/OMEX archives are zip files that contain an additional manifest file that indicates the format (e.g., CellML, CSV, SBML, SED-ML, PNG, etc.) of each file in the archive. This simple format can capture a broad range of projects. The format also provides authors the flexibility to organize their projects as appropriate.

principles.principle: COMBINE/OMEX archives should contain SED-ML experiment descriptions and models in standard formats (e.g., SBML, BNGL).
principles.evidence: Command-line application and high-level utilities for reading, writing, validating, and executing [COMBINE/OMEX format](https://combinearchive.org/) files that contain descriptions of simulations in [Simulation Experiment Description Markup Language](https://sed-ml.org/) (SED-ML) format with models in formats such as the [BioNetGen Language](https://bionetgen.org) (BNGL) and the [Systems Biology Markup Language](http://sbml.org) (SBML).

principles.principle: Before publishing a run, verify the archive includes all relevant files, results and metadata are correct, and visualizations and thumbnail display properly.
principles.evidence: We recommend verifying the following aspects of runs: The COMBINE/OMEX archive includes all relevant files. The simulation behaved as expected and the results are visualized as expected. The simulation accurately reproduces biological behavior. The simulation project metadata is accurate and complete. The thumbnail image displays correctly.

principles.principle: Validation tools should check the archive manifest, model files, SED-ML files, metadata, and images and report errors.
principles.evidence: The tool will validate the contents of the archive and report any errors. The interface provides a report of the validation results, including validation of the model file, SED-ML file, metadata, archive manifest, and any images presented in the archive.

principles.principle: Reports and plots produced from SED-ML documents follow specific table-row/heading conventions tied to SED-ML elements.
principles.evidence: For reports, the rows of each data table will represent the data sets ( sedml:dataSet ) outlined in the SED-ML definition of the report. The heading of each row will be the label of the corresponding data set. For plots, the rows of each data table will represent the data generators ( sedml:dataGenerator ) outlined in the SED-ML definition of the plot. The heading of each row will be the id of the corresponding data generator.

principles.principle: COMBINE/OMEX archives are suitable for capturing a broad range of simulation projects across many modeling frameworks, algorithms, and model formats (and are used as examples/test-suite materials).
principles.evidence: This directory is a collection of example [COMBINE/OMEX archives](https://combinearchive.org/) that describe simulations of biological models. As detailed below, the archives in this directory involve a variety of modeling frameworks (e.g., logical, constraint-based), simulation algorithms (e.g., CVODE, SSA), and model formats (e.g., BNGL, SBML). All of the simulations in the archives in this directory are described using the [Simulation Experiment Description Markup Language (SED-ML)](https://sed-ml.org).

standards.name: BioSimulators tool specification (biosimulators.json)
standards.abstract: This specification describes how to package and publish simulation tools (command-line and containerized) so they can be used by the BioSimulations platform. The research objects are simulation tools / simulators (software) that execute COMBINE/OMEX archives containing SED-ML simulation experiments; recordings/data are simulation outputs (reports and plots) saved to files (HDF5 for tabular results, PDF for plots inside a zip). The standard is maintained by the BioSimulations project (docs at docs.biosimulations.org and the BioSimulators GitHub organization). It defines the expected metadata keys for simulator submissions (YAML/JSON keys used when creating GitHub issues or specifications), the required/optional attributes and methods for a Python API wrapper, the command-line interface arguments and expected output file formats, and fields used by the automated test/validation workflows. The specification addresses how to annotate capabilities, how to structure the Docker image and CLI, how to format reports and logs, and how to submit/validate simulators to the BioSimulators registry.

classification.rationale: The source material repeatedly presents concrete named fields and configuration keys (e.g., YAML/JSON keys for submissions such as name, version, specificationsUrl, validateImage, commitSimulator; command-line arguments like -i/--archive and -o/--out-dir; API attribute __version__ with type str). These are field-level definitions with explicit names and types or constrained formats, so the source functions as a metadata table/schema rather than prose guidance or a procedural DAG.

standards.name: BioSimulators execution log format for COMBINE/OMEX
standards.abstract: This standard concerns execution logs produced by simulation runs packaged as COMBINE/OMEX archives and exchanged via the BioSimulators API. The recordings are JSON-formatted logs (referenced as simulationRunLog_CombineArchiveLog) submitted to and retrieved from an API for validation, storage, and retrieval. The material here is an OpenAPI description of the API endpoints maintained by BioSimulators (see api.biosimulations.org), documenting operations to validate, get, create, and replace simulation-run logs, health checks, and related permission and size constraints.

It does not present a field-level metadata table nor an ordered workflow/DAG; instead it describes actions and requirements (what the API does and expects), which correspond to reporting/behavioral principles rather than a structured metadata table or a DAG.

standards.name: Kinetic Simulation Algorithm Ontology (KiSAO)
standards.abstract: KiSAO (Kinetic Simulation Algorithm Ontology) is an ontology that catalogues algorithms used to simulate and analyze biological models, together with their characteristics, input parameters, and outputs. The ontology is published and maintained by the SED-ML Editors and distributed in OWL format (with derived CSV/RDF representations available via BioPortal/OLS). The project provides guidelines for contributing new terms (including required annotations and URI conventions), a Python library for programmatic access and algorithm substitutability utilities, and a documented release process that publishes new versions to BioPortal and PyPI.

classification.rationale: The source material is an ontology (OWL files) and supporting repository documentation (README, CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, CHANGELOG, Python package docs). It is not a metadata table of named fields with types nor a sequential workflow; the repository provides prose descriptions, policies, and guidelines (instructions for contributors and usage), so the PRINCIPLE type best matches the actual structure.

principles.principle: Purpose / scope of KiSAO
principles.evidence: The Kinetic Simulation Algorithm Ontology (KiSAO) is an ontology of algorithms for simulating and analyzing biological models, as well as the characteristics of these algorithms, their input parameters, and their outputs. In addition, KiSAO captures relationships among algorithms, their parameters, and their outputs.

principles.principle: Ontology format and availability
principles.evidence: KiSAO is developed in the OWL format. The current release of KiSAO is available in OWL format [here](https://github.com/SED-ML/KiSAO/tree/dev/kisao.owl). KiSAO is available in CSV and RDF/XML formats from [BioPortal](https://bioportal.bioontology.org/ontologies/KISAO).

principles.principle: Maintainers / contact
principles.evidence: contact: [{ "name": "SED-ML Editors", "email": "sed-ml-editors@googlegroups.com" }]

principles.principle: How to edit the ontology (contribution workflow)
principles.evidence:
The ontology should be edited using the [Protégé](https://protege.stanford.edu/) ontology editor.

1. Fork this repository.
2. Use Protégé to edit [`kisao.owl`](kisao.owl).
3. The following attributes should be specified for each new term (with the data types in parantheses):
   - `rdfs:label` (`language:en`): primary name of the term  
   - `skos:definition` (`language:en`): description of the term
   - `dcterms:creator`: (`language:en`): initial of the investigator who created the term (e.g., `JRK`)
   - `dcterms:created`: (`xsd:date`): date the term was created (e.g., `2021-06-03`)
4. The following attributes can also be used to describe new terms:
   - `isOrganizational` (`xsd:boolean`): set this to `true` if the term is an abstract concept (i.e. shouldn't be used in a SED-ML document; only its children should be used in SED-ML documents)
   - `skos:altLabel` (`language:en`): synonym for the term
   - `rdfs:seeAlso` (`xsd:anyURI`): URL for more information about the term (e.g., `https://identifiers.org/doi/XYZ`)
      - `rdfs:comment` (`language:en`): human-readable citation for the URL
   - `isImplementedIn` (`xsd:anyURI`): URL for a simulation tool which supports the term (e.g., `https://identifiers.org/biosimulators/tellurium`)
      - `rdfs:comment` (`language:en`): name of the simulation tool (e.g., `tellurium`)
5. Save your changes to `kisao.owl`.

principles.principle: Conventions for identifiers and labels
principles.evidence:
Contributions to KiSAO should adhere to the following conventions:

- URIs of terms should follow the pattern `http://www.biomodels.net/kisao/KISAO#KISAO_\d{7,7}`
- URIs should be assigned sequentially, starting from the greatest id
- Labels should start with a lowercase letter, except for proper names such as the name of a person (e.g., `Gillespie's Algorithm`)
- Labels should not contain special characters or brackets

principles.principle: Release process for new versions
principles.evidence:
Releasing new versions

1. Revise [`kisao.owl`](kisao.owl).
2. Add description of changes to [`CHANGELOG.md`](CHANGELOG.md).
3. Increment the version in [`kisao.owl`](kisao.owl) and [`kisao_full.owl`](kisao_full.owl).
3. Increment the version in [`libkisao/python/kisao/_version.py`](libkisao/python/kisao/_version.py).
4. Commit and push the new version (e.g., `git add kisao.owl kisao_full.owl; git commit -m "..."; git push`).
5. Tag the new version (e.g., `git tag 2.14`).
6. Push the new tag (`git push --tags`).
7. Pushing this tag will trigger a GitHub action which will perform the following tasks: 
   * Merge the changes into the deploy branch
   * Create a new GitHub release
   * Submit the new version to BioPortal
   * Submit the new version of the Python package to PyPI
   * Compile the documentation of the Python package and push it to this repository.

principles.principle: License
principles.evidence: KiSAO is released under [Artistic License 2.0](LICENSE).

principles.principle: Browsing and programmatic access
principles.evidence:
KiSAO can be browsed through [BioPortal](https://bioportal.bioontology.org/ontologies/KISAO) and [OLS](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ols/ontologies/kisao).

A package is available for working with KiSAO in Python: https://github.com/SED-ML/KiSAO/tree/dev/libkisao/python.

principles.principle: Ontology relationships (example object property)
principles.evidence: 'has characteristic' links algorithms to the characteristics they possess.

principles.principle: Python utilities: substitutability matrix
principles.evidence:
To generate a matrix of the substitutability among algorithms, install this package with the `substitutability-matrix` option:
```
pip install kisao[substitutability-matrix]
```

A matrix of the substitutability of algorithms catalogued by KiSAO is available [here](https://github.com/SED-ML/KiSAO/blob/dev/libkisao/python/docs/algorithm-substitutability.csv).

standards.notes: I classified this standard as PRINCIPLE because the repository contents are documentation and ontology files (OWL) that provide prose guidance, conventions, and contributor instructions rather than a metadata table or an ordered workflow. Extracted principles include both high-level purpose statements and concrete contributor/release rules; each principle above is supported by a verbatim quote from the provided source files.
